name: Jade Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. I like this sort of thing, actually, I'm always reading about where farming's going.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Sam and I run Hill End, a 60-hectare tenant farm with 150 dairy goats, some cereals and a field of vegetables. I do the goat side: milking at five, the kids, the cheese room in the morning, then the farm shop in the afternoons on Fridays and Saturdays. Sam does the arable and most of the shop. I love making cheese; the milking at five every single day is the part that grinds you down.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're doing well for a small farm. The cheese sells to delis in town and the shop does good trade, and we've got about ten months of costs saved plus the machinery we own outright. I use AI tools every day, for the books, the shop's social media, the milk records and even tweaking cheese recipes. No kids yet, we're both twenty-seven and too busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That'd surprise me, but okay. I use it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy, not magic. AI already writes my farm shop posts and balances the books, and if that's all it ever does, I'm still two evenings a week better off. I'd probably say that in a post on the shop's page, with a picture of a goat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means our plans carry on. The farm's doing fine, savings are good, there are plenty of farms nearby if the tenancy ever ended. The only real pressure is the tenancy renewal in four years, and that's a council thing, not an AI thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing and keep using the tools I've got. I'd look at whether the AI can help with ordering for the shop, since that eats an hour a week. And we'd keep saving for a bigger tenancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit underwhelmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the tenancy renewal.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council reviews it every ten years. We've done well, so I think we're fine, but you never know with councils. If we lost it, we'd have savings and goats and nowhere to put them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the next thing you'd like AI to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plan the kidding dates better, maybe, so the milk flow is steadier through the winter.

I'd say it saves me **two evenings** a week on posts and books.
think: Privately our **farm plans** carry on as before.
The real pressure is the **tenancy renewal** in four years, not AI.
do: Keep using AI for the **books** and the shop's social media.
Try AI for **shop ordering**, which eats an hour a week.
S0.quote: AI already writes my farm shop posts and balances the books, and if that's all it ever does, I'm still two evenings a week better off.
fieldNote: She's a **daily AI user** who finds the plateau a small letdown.
Her existing worry is the **council tenancy**, unrelated to AI.
She runs a **small business** with real assets and savings.

steps.text: Try AI for ordering stock in the Hill End farm shop
Keep milking and making cheese as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That's the one I'd put money on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms can use AI to compete with big ones for the first time. I'd say that at the farmers' market and online. My partner Sam and I spend Sunday nights on invoices, so software doing the office side of the goat farm sounds like a gift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for us. My work is mostly hands-on, so the robots coming slowly gives me time, and the office stuff going to software is a pure saving. The thing I'd watch is the delis in town, because if their staff get cut, they might buy less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within a few months I'd move all the invoicing and stock to an AI system. I'd use it to set up online cheese sales with delivery, which we've never had time for. And I'd pay attention to robotic milking for goats, which is a few years behind cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited. Like the first warm day in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you think online sales would bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a fifth more turnover in the first year, if I get the postage right. Cheese is fussy to post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone around you who'd be hurt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our friend Hannah does bookkeeping for half the farms round here. That's exactly the work on that card.

I'd say handing the **office side** to software sounds like a gift.
think: Privately it's **good for us**, since my work is mostly hands-on.
I'd watch the **delis in town**, which might buy less if their staff are cut.
do: Move all **invoicing and stock** to an AI system within months.
Set up **online cheese sales** with delivery.
Keep an eye on **robotic milking** for goats.
S1.quote: My partner Sam and I spend Sunday nights on invoices, so software doing the office side of the goat farm sounds like a gift.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a **leveller** for small farms.

She names **Hannah**, a local bookkeeper, as someone likely to be hurt.

steps.text: Move Hill End's invoicing and stock records to an AI system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast. That's before the tenancy renewal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge chance and a huge risk, and the government needs to keep people's incomes up while it settles. I'd say small businesses need help to buy robots, not just the giants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the robots coming in 2031 might suit me, because milking at five is my least favourite job. The goats don't care who milks them, but the people buying my cheese care whether they've still got a job in town. If half of them lose their jobs in 2028, our shop and the delis feel it straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd cut what we don't need and build the savings to a year and a half. I'd shift sales to things people buy even when money's tight, like goat milk and eggs, not just fancy cheese. And I'd plan to buy a milking robot around 2031, when they're proven on goats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for the goats, for the customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new cheese cave we were planning, which was thirty thousand. That waits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be one of the people losing out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the shop's takings drop by a third, we'd be tight but not sunk. It's the not knowing how far it drops that gets me.

say: I'd say it's a **huge chance** and a huge risk at once.
I'd say **small businesses** need help to buy robots, not just giants.
think: Privately robots in 2031 might take my **least favourite** job, the five o'clock milking.
The danger is **customers in town** losing jobs in 2028 and spending less.
do: Put the **thirty thousand** cheese cave on hold.
Build savings up to **eighteen months** of costs.
Plan to buy a **milking robot** around 2031.
feel: I feel **anxious**, more for customers than for the goats.
S2.quote: The goats don't care who milks them, but the people buying my cheese care whether they've still got a job in town.
fieldNote: Her risk is **demand**, not her own labour, which is unusual for a farmer.
She'd welcome **robots** for the worst part of her job.
She has **real control** through savings and a flexible business.

steps.text: Put the thirty thousand pound cheese cave on hold
Build savings up to eighteen months of farm costs
Buy a goat milking robot around 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a sensible amount of warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for farms to plan ahead, and I'd be telling every young farmer I know to get ready. I'd probably run a talk at the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out fine if I'm a bit ahead. I'd buy a goat milking robot in 2033, the year before everyone else does, while the second-hand ones are still cheap. The thinking AI would already be running our books and orders by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd visit two farms abroad that already use goat robots, and I'd start saving towards one. I'd put money into the shop, maybe a café, so people come for the experience. And I'd push the council to renew the tenancy early, for fifteen years instead of ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly in a good way. Busy-minded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would people come for a café if their incomes are under pressure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. A cup of tea and a cheese scone is still cheap. People cut the holiday before they cut the treat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sam think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would say I'm getting ahead of myself. Then he'd build the café.

say: I'd say farms can **plan ahead** and young farmers should get ready.
I'd give a talk at the **young farmers' club**.
think: Privately I come out **fine** if I'm a bit ahead.

feel: I feel **uneasy** in a busy-minded, mostly good way.
S3.quote: I'd buy a goat milking robot in 2033, the year before everyone else does, while the second-hand ones are still cheap.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **get ahead** of neighbours, which suits her adaptability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good version: there's time for everyone to get ready. I'd say that cheerfully, but I'd still say people need help to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think we'd do well. With ten years I'd rather the robot milked the goats at five in the morning and I made the cheese by hand at nine. Handmade cheese will be worth more when everything else is made by machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as now and keep growing the cheese business. I'd put money into a bigger cheese room around 2030. And I'd buy the robot when it's cheap and proven, maybe 2038.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-seven in 2036. Does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it easier. By then we'd have kids at school and a settled business. Change is easier when you're not starting from scratch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council selling the farm. That's always the thing that could go wrong, robots or not.

I'd still say people need **help to retrain**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because our customers in town would lose jobs before we had time to adjust. I'm not scared of robots in the dairy; I'm scared of a town where nobody has the money for good cheese. What would help is the government keeping people's incomes up during the change, and grants for small farms to buy robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the council tenancy, and honestly that worries me more than any robot. A secure lease would help in every one of your pictures.

Her lasting worry is the **council tenancy**, not robots.
